strengths: Introduces Vlaser-6M, a large-scale embodied reasoning dataset and data engine spanning grounding, planning, spatial reasoning, and in-domain robot QA, with open-source model and data promised.
Extensive evaluation across 12 embodied reasoning benchmarks shows strong performance and state-of-the-art results on several tasks (e.g., planning, grounding, spatial reasoning).
Systematic study of VLM-to-VLA transfer compares multiple data streams and identifies in-domain robot QA as more effective for downstream policy learning than out-of-domain embodied reasoning data.
Achieves state-of-the-art average success on WidowX SimplerEnv and competitive results on Google Robot, with clear hyperparameters and training details.
Provides qualitative examples and in-domain data templates that could aid reproducibility and future research.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: Vlaser largely combines an existing InternVL3 VLM backbone with a flow-matching action expert and standard SFT; the main new component is data curation.

The central domain-shift claim is not rigorously isolated. Comparisons confound data source, quantity, generation model (Qwen2.5-VL/GPT-4o), and task distribution; no controlled ablation at fixed token/quality is provided.
Evaluation is entirely in simulation (SimplerEnv), with no real-robot validation; success rates lack confidence intervals or seed variance, making small differences hard to interpret.
The averaged metric in Table 1 is not well-defined or justified, and aggregating raw percentages across heterogeneous benchmarks can be misleading.

Data quality and bias are not fully addressed: in-domain QA and planning data are generated by other VLMs/LLMs, with filtering and successful-trajectory selection that may introduce distillation bias and limit diversity.
On Google Robot, the method is not state-of-the-art across all task variants (e.g., Magma has higher variant aggregation average), so claims of competitive/SOTA performance are somewhat overstated.
Writing clarity and reproducibility details are inconsistent, with several typos, confusing model variant descriptions, and reference formatting issues.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and relevant problem: bridging embodied VLM reasoning and downstream VLA policy learning.
It curates a large Vlaser-6M dataset spanning embodied QA, grounding, spatial reasoning, planning, and in-domain simulation data, which could be a useful community resource if released.
The evaluation covers a broad set of 12 embodied reasoning benchmarks plus SimplerEnv WidowX and Google Robot tasks.
Vlaser shows substantial gains over its InternVL3 base models on many upstream embodied reasoning benchmarks.
The paper reports a practically relevant observation that out-of-domain embodied reasoning data may not transfer as well as in-domain robot data, highlighting domain shift in VLA training.
The authors promise open-source code, model weights, and data, which could support reproducibility and future research.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the method is essentially supervised fine-tuning of InternVL3 with a pi0-style flow-matching action expert; the data engine aggregates and reannotates existing datasets rather than introducing a fundamentally new approach.

Potential train/test contamination is a serious concern: training data sources such as Paco-Lavis, Pixmo-Points, and RefSpatial overlap with evaluation benchmarks such as Paco-Lavis, Pixmo-Points, and RefSpatial-Bench, but held-out splits and decontamination procedures are not clearly described.

The claimed 'systematic analysis' of VLM-to-VLA transfer is underdeveloped and not sufficiently controlled: only a few coarse data variants are tested on one model size, without full data-mixture ablations, multiple seeds, or scaling analyses.
Downstream robot evaluation is entirely in simulation (SimplerEnv), with no real-robot validation, despite claims about real-world relevance and state-of-the-art robot performance.

Robot results are inconsistent and not uniformly state-of-the-art: Vlaser alone often does not clearly improve over InternVL3-2B, while Vlaser-QA/Grounding gains may be driven by target-domain Bridge/Simulation QA data rather than general embodied reasoning.

Baseline comparisons are not apples-to-apples: many numbers are copied from prior papers under different training and evaluation protocols, and there are no controlled reimplementations or statistical significance tests.
The claim of state-of-the-art WidowX performance with Vlaser-QA may be confounded by in-domain data generated from the same environment or task distribution as the evaluation.
Reproducibility is incomplete: key details are missing for data generation prompts, splits, action-expert architecture, state/action tokenization, training compute, and random seeds.

The central insight—that in-domain data helps downstream control more than out-of-domain reasoning data—is intuitive and already broadly understood, so the contribution is not strong enough to compensate for the methodological weaknesses.
Writing and presentation have many issues, including typos, malformed citations, repeated references, unclear notation, and awkward phrasing, which hinder clarity and credibility.

strengths: Addresses an important gap between upstream VLM-based embodied reasoning and downstream VLA policy learning.
Introduces a large, diverse dataset (Vlaser-6M) covering embodied QA, grounding, spatial reasoning, planning, and in-domain simulation data.
Comprehensive evaluation across 12 embodied reasoning benchmarks and two SimplerEnv robot manipulation tasks.
Strong empirical results: Vlaser-2B/8B outperform or match larger models on several benchmarks, and Vlaser-QA achieves high success on WidowX.
Provides a useful empirical finding that in-domain robot data is more effective than out-of-domain embodied reasoning data for downstream VLA, highlighting the domain shift problem.
Clear two-stage training recipe with a flow-matching action expert.
Promises open-source release of code, model, and data.
weaknesses: Potential train/test overlap: training data includes Paco-Lavis, Pixmo-Points, RefSpatial, and other datasets that are also used as evaluation benchmarks, with no clarification of data splits, undermining the claimed state-of-the-art embodied reasoning results.

Unfair comparisons: Vlaser-QA is pretrained on in-domain Bridge QA data, while baselines such as pi0 are cited from external sources under different training/evaluation protocols; this makes the downstream VLA comparisons inconclusive.

Inconsistent ablation: Table 3 shows that Vlaser (full Vlaser-6M data) performs worse than Vlaser-Grounding, Vlaser-QA, and Vlaser-Spatial on Google Robot tasks, contradicting the claim that incorporating all data types leads to improvement.

Limited technical novelty: the architecture is InternVL3 plus an existing flow-matching action expert, and the dataset is largely an aggregation of public datasets plus synthetic in-domain QA; the main contribution is an empirical study.
No statistical significance testing or error bars for the VLA success rates; many reported differences are small and may not be reliable.
Technical errors and inconsistencies, e.g., setting the flow-matching integration step size δ = 10 (which would exceed the time horizon) while later stating 10 inference steps.
Reproducibility concerns: code, model, and data are only promised to be released; no details on train/test splits, data filtering, or validation of synthetic data quality are provided.

The 'systematic analysis' is narrow: only one in-domain QA variant is tested on WidowX, no combined all-data ablation is shown, and the out-of-domain failure is explained only by general domain shift.
No discussion of ethical or safety considerations for robot learning, which is important for embodied AI systems.
Writing quality suffers from numerous typos, inconsistent naming, and malformed references, reducing clarity.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across 12 embodied reasoning benchmarks and three simulation benchmarks, with strong aggregate results including best average on embodied reasoning and state-of-the-art performance on WidowX.

Provides a systematic study of how different VLM pretraining data types affect downstream VLA policy learning, yielding the useful empirical insight that in-domain robot data is more effective than out-of-domain embodied reasoning data for downstream control.
Introduces a large-scale Vlaser-6M data engine with detailed data construction, filtering, and quality-control pipelines, and promises to release model weights, data, and code.
Technically sound integration of an InternVL3 backbone with a flow-matching action expert, leveraging recent VLM and VLA design choices.
The domain-shift observation between internet/embodied reasoning benchmarks and real robot observation domains is valuable for future embodied foundation model design.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core model largely supervised-fine-tunes InternVL3 and adds a pi0-style flow-matching action expert, while the dataset is mostly curated from existing datasets with synthetic QA generation.

The central claim of synergistic embodied reasoning and control is not fully tested: VLA experiments do not evaluate the full Vlaser-6M combination of out-of-domain and in-domain data, and Vlaser-All appears to use only in-domain data, so synergy is not directly demonstrated.
Downstream VLA experiments only use 2B models and are entirely simulation-based; no real-robot results are provided, and no 8B VLA results are reported, limiting the generality of the conclusions.

The key negative finding that out-of-domain embodied reasoning does not transfer to downstream VLA may be confounded by data quantity, visual domain shift, and VLA fine-tuning details; controlled experiments isolating domain alignment from reasoning ability are missing.

There is a potential fairness/leakage concern because in-domain QA data is generated from the same simulation platforms used for evaluation, and train/test task separation for the simulation benchmarks is not clearly described.

Vlaser is not best on all individual embodied reasoning benchmarks, e.g., ERQA, MMSI-Bench, and EB-Habitat, so the state-of-the-art claim is driven by normalized average performance, and some baselines may not be optimized for the embodied benchmarks.

strengths: Constructs a large and diverse embodied dataset (Vlaser-6M) by aggregating and re-annotating many existing sources (grounding, spatial, QA, planning, in-domain simulation), which could be a useful community resource if properly released and documented.

Provides a systematic, controlled ablation on the WidowX, Google Robot, and RoboTwin benchmarks comparing OOD-only, QA-only, spatial-only, grounding-only, and combined in-domain VLM pretraining, which is more thorough than many comparable VLA papers.
Reports results across a broad set of 12 embodied reasoning benchmarks and three closed-loop simulation suites, and commits to open-sourcing weights, data, and code, which aids reproducibility.
The empirical observation that internet-scale OOD embodied-reasoning gains do not necessarily transfer to downstream VLA control is at least a clearly-stated, testable claim with supporting numbers.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The VLM is a supervised fine-tune of InternVL3, and the action expert is explicitly described as 'following (Intelligence et al., 2025)' with flow matching + MoE, i.e., essentially the pi0-style design. The 'data engine' largely curates, re-labels, and re-packages existing public datasets with LLM-generated QA, rather than introducing a new method, loss, or learning paradigm.

Serious evaluation validity concerns. Several benchmarks used for evaluation (Paco-Lavis, Pixmo-Points, RefSpatial) are also listed as training-data sources (Paco-LaVIS, Pixmo-Points, RefSpatial), and RoboPoint is both a training source and the origin of the Where2Place benchmark. The paper does not describe train/test split handling, so the claimed SOTA on these benchmarks is not credible as reported.

The in-domain data used for the downstream VLA study is generated from SimplerEnv/RoboTwin, i.e., the exact environments used for closed-loop evaluation. Training on the evaluation environment while baselines do not receive this data confounds the 'SOTA on WidowX' claim; the observed in-domain gains are at least partly explained by test-distribution supervision rather than a generalizable insight.

The headline finding ('in-domain data helps downstream VLA, OOD reasoning data does not') is unsurprising and largely anticipated by prior co-training/robot-data work; the framing that Vlaser 'bridges' reasoning and control is actually contradicted by the result that reasoning-benchmark gains do not transfer to control.

No real-robot experiments. All control results are in simulation. The paper acknowledges this, but for a VLA paper claiming deployment relevance, this is a substantive gap rather than a minor limitation.

Manuscript quality is poor. Numerous typos and errors (e.g., 'CharVLA-2B', 'ReboBrain2-0-3B', 'Velbrain-7B', inconsistent 'VLABench/VLA-Bench'), duplicated/mislabeled references (Gemini Robotics Team appears as both 2025b and 2025c with identical content; 'Team et al. (2023) BAAI RoboBrain Team...'), garbled bibliography numbering, and odd capitalization in headings ('PERFORMANCE ON EMBodied REASONING CAPABILITY'). This suggests insufficient editing.

Method section is thin on architectural detail (action-expert size, parameter sharing, attention masking, state/action tokenization), making reproduction of the policy harder than the reproducibility statement implies.

Some qualitative/grounding outputs appear erroneous (e.g., the RoboTwin grounding example returns identical duplicate points [565,775],[565,775]), and no quantitative error analysis of such failure modes is given.

Baseline comparisons are not apples-to-apples in several places: differing parameter counts, differing pretraining data (including in-domain synthetic data unavailable to baselines), and results borrowed from other papers with potentially different evaluation protocols, without controlling for these factors.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale, multi-source dataset (Vlaser-6M) and a systematic data engine covering embodied QA, grounding, spatial reasoning, planning, and in-domain simulation data, which could be valuable to the community.
Conducts extensive evaluations on 12 embodied reasoning benchmarks and multiple simulation platforms, showing strong SOTA or competitive results and providing many baselines.

Performs a useful systematic ablation on which VLM pretraining data streams help downstream VLA fine-tuning, with the interesting finding that OOD embodied reasoning benchmarks do not directly translate to better control, whereas in-domain data does.
Integrates a flow-matching action expert with a VLM backbone and achieves strong performance on WidowX and competitive results on Google Robot and RoboTwin.
Reproducibility is supported by detailed training hyperparameters, data generation procedures, and a commitment to open-source code, model, and data.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the architecture largely follows InternVL3 plus a pi0-style flow-matching action expert, and the dataset mostly aggregates existing datasets plus generated QA using off-the-shelf models.

The central 'synergistic embodied reasoning' claim is not fully supported: OOD embodied reasoning pretraining alone does not improve downstream VLA performance, and it is unclear whether it is necessary when combined with in-domain data.
Missing controlled ablation: there is no comparison of InternVL3-2B fine-tuned directly on in-domain QA, so the effect of Vlaser-OOD pretraining in the full pipeline is not isolated.
Evaluation is simulation-only (SimplerEnv, RoboTwin) with no real-robot experiments, leaving real-world applicability and robustness unverified.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: Table 1 has a confusing header and apparently missing benchmark column, Table 4 formatting is broken, and naming is inconsistent across Vlaser/Vlaser-OOD/Vlaser-All variants.

The SOTA claims rely on a simple average across heterogeneous benchmarks; some baselines are general-purpose models not specifically fine-tuned for embodied tasks, and the normalization procedure is not fully explained.
